abstract: Rapid training of terrain-aware locomotion requires both high simulation throughput and trajectories that remain informative for learning. Keeping Isaac Gym simulation, policy inference, observations, rewards, and proximal policy optimization on one GPU reduces CPU-GPU transfers. A performance-adaptive curriculum raises difficulty after successful traversal and lowers it after insufficient progress by relocating robots among prebuilt terrain tiles, avoiding regeneration. A single policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights to follow motion commands. With 4,096 robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 policy updates, an ANYmal C policy trains in under 20 minutes on an i9-11900k/RTX A6000 workstation. This speed depends on retaining adequate consecutive rollout steps per robot: increasing parallelism at fixed batch size eventually shortens trajectories enough to impair learning. Simulation tests show nearly complete traversal success without base contact on stairs up to 0.2 m, declining success on randomized obstacles, and failed climbing beyond 25-degree slopes. The fixed policy also negotiates stairs and obstacles on hardware, but imperfect elevation maps reduce robustness, prompting a 0.6 m/s command limit. Together, these results establish rapid training and physical deployment under the reported configuration, bounded by rollout duration and terrain sensing.
methods: Proximal policy optimization (PPO) uses a critic to estimate an infinite-horizon discounted return, so failure or goal completion and time-limit resets require different treatment. Failures and completed goals can be anticipated from the state; a time-out cannot, because observations omit episode time. Treating a time-out as terminal would therefore remove continuation value for a reason the critic cannot observe, truncating its target rather than reflecting task completion. The environment flags time-outs separately and augments their rewards with the critic's own discounted prediction of future return, bootstrapping the interrupted trajectory's target instead of assigning zero continuation value. This prediction concerns the trajectory cut short, not the episode started after reset. Episodes last up to 20 seconds and span multiple short rollout batches because environments are not reset after each policy update. Time-outs can consequently occur inside a batch and must be handled wherever they occur, not merely at collection boundaries.
results: Figure 4 shows that faster data collection improves the reward-time trade-off only while per-robot trajectories remain long enough for learning. The comparison removes the curriculum, reduces maximum stair and obstacle difficulty, and reports mean episode reward and standard deviation over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. At fixed batch size, more robots mean fewer consecutive steps per robot: training becomes faster, but reward drops sharply at excessive parallelism. The authors explain this drop through insufficient temporal information for advantage estimation; they tentatively attribute the smaller reward decline at low robot counts to reduced sample diversity. Throughput scales nearly linearly to about 4,000 robots before gains slow. Larger batches increase reward and permit more robots before deterioration, at greater training cost. The million-sample, 20,000-robot baseline attains the highest reward but takes longer to train. Thus, about 2,048-4,096 robots with roughly 100,000-200,000 samples per batch offer the reported compromise on this simplified task, balancing trajectory length, diversity, and throughput rather than licensing unlimited parallelism.
notes: Abstract links GPU residency to reduced transfers and tile relocation to adaptive difficulty without regeneration (Sections 2.1 and 3.1); training and deployment claims retain the workstation and sensing limits (Sections 4.2-4.3). Methods explains why unobserved time-outs need critic bootstrapping across batches (Section 2.2.2). Results connects fixed batch size to shorter rollouts and the Figure 4 trade-off; explanations are author interpretations, not isolated causal findings. Hardware transfer also uses simulation randomization and an actuator model. Exact plotted rewards, timing coordinates, and hardware trial counts are not supplied and are not inferred; the rollout constraint is task-specific.
